chapter: Bird's world, singers and the new music
title: 'Not an old diehard': Bird's lesson and the avant-garde
summary: He's open to anything that sounds good.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Because I used to give those guys hell back then when I played out in California, and they didn't like nothin' I was doing. They didn't want to hear nothin' about McGhee. And I know that I what I was doing was right, because I was playing with some of the greatest musicians in the world, with Coleman Hawkins and Oscar Pettiford and them... They

ain't jiving. They're musicians. You know what I mean? But the people out there in California, they couldn't understand what I was trying to do. I'd say, "Well, I ain't trying to do no more than just play music. That's all I'm trying to do. I ain't tryin' to be the greatest thing that ever happened. All I want to do is be able to play." Bird taught me that. He taught, "Maggie, whatever you've got to do, you got to play. Whatever you do, you make sure what you're doing is correct. He hipped me to that point.

Well, what kind of an analogy can you draw between the new music of then and, say, the new music of the Sixties and Seventies and on to today, where they many times have followed what Coltrane was doing when he went outside and just seemed to be playing...

Well, I don't know. What can you say, you know? Maybe it's good and maybe it's bad. I don't know. I don't know what it is, really. But I dig a man if a man can go out there and make it sound good. I don't care what he's doing. As long as he sounds good, he ain't go no complaints -- or he shouldn't get any complaints anyway. But now, if he goes out there and sounds bad, then naturally they're going to come home. Anything bad, it's going to come right
back at you. But if it's good, it will come back at you, too.
